extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, or readers of classical mechanics and fluid dynamics (Newtonian mechanics)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted theorems and corollaries about resistance in pendulums, motion in fluids, and projectile drag from a classical-mechanics treatise (propositions on cycloidal motion, scaling laws, resistance scaling, shapes of least resistance, and efflux).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXX (Theorem XXIII): Cycloid arc difference equals area of perpendiculars
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line aB equals the cycloid arc described by an oscillating body, and perpendiculars DK to each point are taken such that they represent resistance at those points relative to gravity (expressed in pendulum length), then the difference between the whole arc of descent and the whole subsequent arc of ascent, multiplied by the semisum of those arcs, equals (approximately) the area occupied by all those perpendiculars DK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: bisect AB in C, represent resisting and gravitational 'forces' by lengths along CD, erect semicircle with center C, compare velocities in vacuum and with resistance by the perpendiculars DE, de, etc. The proposition provides a geometric relation between arc differences in oscillatory motion and the integrated perpendiculars that represent resistance; it yields practical formulae (see corollaries) for relating measured arc differences to resistive force magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXX — Corollary: Resistance at lowest point proportional to area ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: The resistance at the lowest point C is to the force of gravity as the area (designated {OP ÷ OQ} IEF) is to the area PINM — i.e. resistance:gravity :: area IEF : area PINM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This corollary interprets the geometric quantities in Prop. XXX as giving a direct proportion for resistance relative to gravity at the equilibrium point; useful for converting measured arc/area quantities into a resistance-to-weight ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXX — Corollary: Maximum resistance condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The resistance is maximal when area PIHR is to area IEF as OR is to OQ — in that case the momentum term (PIGR - Y) vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a geometric criterion for when resistive loss attains a maximum (the case where the integrated momentum decrement becomes zero).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXX — Corollary: Local velocity vs resistance relation in cycloid
rubrics_metrics.description: The velocity at individual points is (approximately) in the inverse (half?) ratio of the resistance; initially it equals the velocity that the body would have at the same cycloidal point if oscillating without any resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a way to infer local velocities from measured resistances or vice versa, referenced to the resistance-free cycloidal motion as baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXI (Theorem XXIV): Proportional change of resistance produces proportional arc-difference change
rubrics_metrics.description: If the resistance in corresponding parts of the arcs described by an oscillating body increases or decreases in a given ratio, then the difference between the arc of descent described and the subsequent arc of ascent will increase or decrease in the same ratio (approximately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: the arc-difference arises from the total retardation due to resistance, so scaling the resistance scales the arc-difference. Used to deduce how varying resistive laws affect measured oscillation amplitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXI — Corollary 1 (resistance ∝ velocity ⇒ arc-difference ∝ arc)
rubrics_metrics.description: If resistance is proportional to velocity, then the difference of the arcs in the same medium is proportional to the total arc described (and conversely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical diagnostic: measured arc-differences scaling linearly with arc length indicate a linear (∝ v) resistive law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXI — Corollary 2 (resistance ∝ velocity^2 ⇒ arc-difference ∝ (arc)^2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If resistance is proportional to the square of the velocity, then that arc-difference is in the duplicate (square) ratio of the total arc; and conversely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental test: if arc-difference scales like the square of arc length, it signals a quadratic velocity-dependence of resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXI — Corollary 3 (general power law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, if resistance is proportional to any power (triplicate or any) of the velocity, then the arc-difference will be in the same power-law ratio of the total arc (and conversely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a general mapping between the velocity-exponent in the resistive law and the exponent observable in arc-difference vs. arc-length measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXI — Corollary 4 (mixed resistance components add correspondingly)
rubrics_metrics.description: If resistance is partly proportional to velocity and partly proportional to its square, then the arc-difference will be partly proportional to the total arc and partly to its square (and conversely); the law of resistance corresponds to the law of differences for arc-lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables decomposition of complex resistances into additive components by observing composite dependencies of arc-differences on arc-length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXI — Corollary 5 (extension to unequal successive arcs)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a pendulum describes unequal successive arcs, one can determine the ratio of increase and decrease of resistance per unit arc length, and so the ratio for larger or smaller velocities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a method to infer how resistance changes with velocity from measurements across nonuniform oscillations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXII (Theorem XXV): Similar system scaling law
rubrics_metrics.description: If two systems consist of equal numbers of similar particles arranged correspondingly and with a given ratio of densities, and they begin to move similarly with times proportional to one another (and particles do not touch except at reflections, nor attract/repel except by accelerative forces proportional to inverse diameters and to squares of velocities), then corresponding particles of the two systems will continue to move similarly with times proportional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A scaling principle: dynamically similar particle systems with scaled densities and suitably scaled forces exhibit geometrically similar motions scaled in time — provides basis for similarity arguments and dimensional-type scaling in fluid/particle systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIII (Theorem XXVI): Resistance scaling law (v^2, diameter^2, density)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the same hypotheses, the resistances of corresponding larger parts of the systems are to one another in a composite ratio formed from the duplicate (square) ratio of their velocities, the duplicate (square) ratio of their diameters, and the ratio of their part-densities (i.e., resistance ∝ v^2 × diameter^2 × density).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument splits resistance into parts from centripetal/centrifugal pairwise forces and from collisions/reflections; both contributions combine to yield the composite scaling. This is the theoretical justification that, in many fluids, drag scales with velocity squared and cross-sectional area and with medium/particle density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIII — Corollary 1 (elastic fluids and projectiles)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the two systems are elastic fluids (like air) with parts at rest relative to each other and if the projectiles are similar and proportional to fluid parts, then projectiles thrown similarly will excite motions in the fluids in proportional times and describe spaces proportional to their diameters; resistances follow the composite ratio above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies scaling law to real projectiles in elastic fluids, establishing proportional relations between similar projectiles in similar fluids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIII — Corollary 2 (approximate v^2 law for very fast projectiles)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the same fluid, a very fast projectile is resisted (approximately) in the duplicate (square) ratio of its velocity. If fluid interparticle motive forces increase in the duplicate ratio of velocities, the resistance is exactly v^2; in the limiting case of no interparticle forces, resistance is exactly v^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives rationale for the common empirical v^2 drag law at high speeds and explains when it is accurate or only approximate depending on interparticle forces in the medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIII — Corollary 4 (resistance ∝ diameter^2 for equal velocities)
rubrics_metrics.description: For similar, equal-density projectiles of equal velocity in an elastic medium whose parts do not flee one another, resistances are (approximately) in the duplicate ratio of their diameters (i.e., ∝ cross-sectional area).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why, for geometrically similar bodies at the same speed, drag scales with area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIII — Corollary 6–9 (effects of particle interactions and fluid constitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: If fluid particles interact (centrifugal forces) or are less lubricous, resistance departs from the pure duplicate-velocity law: (6) stronger mutual centrifugal forces make projectiles harder to move (resistance falls less rapidly than v^2 with speed reduction); (7) centrifugal-force-related increase in resistance is less important for larger bodies; (8) v^2 law is more accurate in fluids of smaller particles (for given elasticity/density); (9) if elasticity arises from other causes than particle centrifugal forces, resistance behavior will differ and generally be larger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These corollaries explain deviations from the ideal v^2 and area laws due to finite particle size, cohesion, or other nonideal elastic properties of real fluids — guidance for when to expect systematic departures from ideal scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIV (Theorem XXVII): Validity when particles touch if very lubricated
rubrics_metrics.description: The conclusions of the previous propositions remain valid even when particles of the systems touch each other, provided the particles are extremely lubricous so that mutual contact does not appreciably impede the motion; any finite difference due to contact can be made arbitrarily small by reducing particle spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extends the scaling and resistance results to dense fluids where particle contact occurs, conditional on high lubrication (i.e., negligible friction/adhesion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXV (Theorem XXVIII): Sphere vs cylinder resistance (ratio)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sphere and a cylinder of the same diameter move equally and very swiftly in a rare elastic medium, with the cylinder advancing along its axis, then the total resistance on the sphere is half the resistance on the cylinder (i.e., sphere's resistance = 1/2 × cylinder's resistance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses imagining medium particles uniformly distributed and computes per-particle impulse differences; leads to practical conclusion that among simple solids of equal diameter, shapes with smaller frontal geometry (sphere) experience less resistance than elongated cylindrical shapes. Follow-up scholium gives constructions for shapes of still lower resistance (paraboloid-like forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium: Shape-design rules for minimal resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: By comparing particle impacts and integrating effects over generating curves, certain revolved shapes (e.g., paraboloid frusta with specific vertex construction, or a body generated by revolving an elliptic/oval curve with tangents making 135° at contact) resist less than other bodies of equal length and breadth; constructions are given for frusta/cones that minimize resistance for a given base and height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives explicit geometric constructions (bisect altitude, etc.) to design frustum/cone/paraboloid shapes that minimize resistance for progressing along axis; suggests application to ship hull design and other engineering contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVI (Prob. VIII): Resistance of a fast-moving sphere in a rare elastic fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides a geometric construction (using a hyperbola and its applied areas) showing that the motion lost by a sphere when it moves through a small element of path CZ, due to medium resistance, is to its whole initial motion approximately as the length CT is to CR. Thus the local fractional loss of motion scales with certain geometric measures determined by medium density and construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derives resistance by comparing to an equivalent cylinder and using reflection assumptions for medium particles; corollaries note that if particles reflect elastically the resistance is larger (by factor up to 2) than if reflections are absent, and explain how knowledge of high-speed resistance can inform low-speed resistance when the law of decrement with velocity is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVII (Prob. IX): Efflux of water through an orifice (Torricelli-type result)
rubrics_metrics.description: If water flows out of a vessel through an orifice, the motion of the effluent corresponds to the weight of the column of water perpendicular to the orifice; the acquired velocity of efflux is related to the head A and the free-fall space S (through mean proportional relations), leading to the result that efflux velocity behaves as if water fell through a certain effective height (classical Torricelli law). For oblique outflow through a channel, the trajectory is a parabola whose latus rectum equals the head of water above the orifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative relations: velocity ratio expressed via mean proportional between head and falling distance S; effective efflux flow is proportional to orifice area; corrections apply for non-ideal (less fluid) water or narrow orifices where particles' finite size slows efflux. Also notes that vertical efflux can reach half the head as an ascent in some constructions; includes qualitative explanation in terms of pressure support by the vessel walls and loss upon opening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVIII (Theorem XXIX): Effect of an immersed sphere on channel flow (throughput vs gap)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sphere is placed in a cylindrical channel through which water flows, the quantity of water flowing per unit time is proportional to the effective aperture (the space between sphere and channel), not exceeding the flow when the sphere is absent; the local velocity with the sphere present cannot exceed the velocity when the sphere is removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats flow as proportional to the cross-sectional area available for transit; assumes an ideal, very fluid medium. Notes reduced flow for more viscous (non-subtle) fluids and uses this to reason about pressure distributions and forces on the vessel sides when efflux occurs.
